conclusion.justification: The report concludes that the highest-quality and most recent evidence does not support probiotics shortening the duration of acute infectious diarrhea, supporting a 'no' answer to the claim. Thus, it rejects the claim based on current high-quality evidence.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
Evidence on this question is mixed, but the highest-quality, most recent evidence supports "no" as the more defensible answer, at least for a clear clinical benefit.

Older, smaller meta-analyses (e.g., the 2006 Lancet meta-analysis) and several pediatric reviews concluded probiotics shorten diarrhea duration by roughly a day (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laninf/article/PIIS1473309906704959/fulltext). However, these were based largely on small, heterogeneous, often industry-linked trials with high risk of bias.

The most authoritative and current evidence is the updated Cochrane systematic review (Collinson et al., 2020), which added large, rigorous, pre-registered RCTs (including a major NEJM trial). This update reversed earlier conclusions: it found no consistent evidence that probiotics shorten time to recovery from acute infectious diarrhea, with the certainty of evidence rated low to very low (https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD003048.pub4/information; https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003048_do-probiotics-help-treat-acute-infectious-diarrhoea; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8166250/).

This shift was driven largely by two large, well-designed U.S. pediatric emergency department trials (including the 2018 NEJM Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG trial) that found no benefit—contradicting earlier positive but smaller/lower-quality studies (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1802598).

Consistent with this, a 2021 analysis in Annals of Emergency Medicine concluded routine probiotic use for acute infectious diarrhea is not recommended (https://www.annemergmed.com/article/S0196-0644(21)00116-5/fulltext).

**Conclusion:** While some older meta-analyses suggested modest benefit, the best current evidence (updated 2020 Cochrane review, incorporating large rigorous trials) does not support probiotics reliably shortening acute infectious diarrhea duration—supporting a "no" answer, albeit with low overall certainty.
